3.3 — Fire Rate: Cooldowns & Time

Last lesson you pressed Play, walked into range, and the turret did not fire a shot — it fired a stream. Nothing you wrote is broken. Your range check is a condition, and it runs every frame, so every frame it called your firing method and the turret fired at your frame rate. Today you give it a memory: a field holding the moment it last fired, and a condition that refuses to fire again until enough time has passed. The fix has more than one honest answer, and you are going to pick one and defend it.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I stop shooting too fast?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

The turret should shoot at me — but not sixty times a second. "Shoot at me, sometimes" is the whole feature, and there is nothing in it yet that a computer can act on.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Notice the player is still inside the radiusThe distance test from 3.1, re-evaluated every frame. It stays true for sixty frames in a row, which is not a bug — it is what a condition is. It is also why the turret hosed bullets in 3.2.Read: your own Update() from 3.1, and the Vector3.Distance row in the quick reference.
  2. write this partRead: the Time.time row in the quick reference, and the deadline you wrote in 1.3 (nextReportTime).
  3. Refuse to fire until enough time has passedOne condition attached to the range check with &&: the clock, against that remembered moment plus the gap you want. Both halves have to be true before the turret may fire.Read: the Cooldown row of the pattern table in the quick reference, and the gate you wrote in 1.3.
  4. Record the new moment the instant a shot leavesOne line, run only when the turret actually fires, and the only thing that closes the gate again. Leave it out and the condition stays true and the frame-rate bug comes straight back inside the fix.Read: the Cooldown row in the pattern table (act, set last = Time.time).

Three of those four parts are code you have already written: the range check is 3.1, the condition is the gate from 1.3, and the line that closes it is that same re-arm line with a different name. Only one part has no precedent in this course. Everything you have made a game remember so far — a coin count, health, whether a door is open — has been a number that changes. A moment is a different kind of number: it means nothing on its own and everything next to the clock it came from, which is why this lesson lives on Time.time.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Fire less often" cannot be looked up. "Compare a timestamp against the current time" can — and you wrote that comparison in 1.3.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

The reading prices four ways to time this action. Which did you choose, and what does your choice cost you — in your own words, not the table's?

Today's memory holds a moment on the clock. If the turret had to charge for a second before each shot, what would that field have to hold instead — and which of the four approaches would you reach for?

In 3.2 you left the turret firing every frame. Nothing in your firing method is wrong, so which line of your own code decided how many times it ran — and is that line a condition or an event?

In 2.2 you gave the Player health: a value declared on the class, changed on one frame, and read again on another. Which part of today's split is that same move — and what is different about the value you store this time?

In 1.3 you learned that Start() runs once and Update() runs every frame. Today's memory needs a value before the first frame ever runs — which method gives it one, and what does the turret do on the first frame the player walks into range if you skip that step?

The Problem: An Action That Happens Too Often ~10 min

Rate limiting is not a game problem. A login form must not accept a thousand attempts a second; a printer must not accept a thousand jobs; a turret must not fire a thousand bullets. The shape of the solution is the same everywhere — remember when the last one happened, and refuse until enough time has passed — and this course handed you every part of it in 1.3.

Press Play and stand inside a turret's radius for five seconds, but watch the Console instead of the screen. Count the lines. That number is not something you wrote: it is how often Update() ran. There is no way to make Update() wait. Any pause you write has to be a test that fails for a while, not a stop — and building that test is the whole of today.

Where this sits in your existing design. In 3.1 you made detection a condition that is re-evaluated every frame, not an event — and you were told that would matter. Here it is. A condition that is true for sixty consecutive frames runs whatever is inside it sixty times. Today's field is the memory that turns that condition into an event.
Read the Docs: Four Ways to Time an Action ~20 min

The engine gives you more than one way to remember when something last happened. Read all four rows, including the last column — the column nobody reads is the one that decides this for you. Then choose, and be ready to defend the choice.

ApproachWhat you storeThe gateWhat it costs you
(a) A Time.time timestamp One float: the moment the last shot happened. Time.time >= lastShot + cooldown One line of state. Forgetting to write the new timestamp turns the gate permanently true — you get the frame-rate bug straight back. A timestamp is only meaningful against the same clock, so anything that pauses or resets time needs thought. Note also what it does not store: it remembers when the last one happened, not how many are owed. A second press inside the window is discarded, not queued.
(b) A countdown timer One float: seconds remaining until the next shot is allowed. timer <= 0f, then timer = cooldown The timer must be decremented by Time.deltaTime on every frame, including frames where the turret is not firing. Forget that and the number quietly stops meaning anything. In exchange, the field reads as "seconds until I can shoot" — which is exactly what a designer wants to see.
(c) InvokeRepeating Nothing at all — the engine holds the schedule. InvokeRepeating(nameof(Fire), 0f, cooldown) Almost no code, and that is the trap: the engine keeps calling your method on cadence whether or not the player is in range, so you still need a range check inside the method. Cancelling is by method name, so renaming the method breaks the cancel silently. Re-tuning the rate at runtime means cancelling and re-invoking.
(d) A coroutine loop A running coroutine handle. while (true) { yield return new WaitForSeconds(t); } The most powerful and the most readable for sequences, and the only one that expresses "charge, then burst, then rest" cleanly. It costs you a StartCoroutine call, a stored handle to stop it, and a second mental model of when your code runs. The yield is what makes it legal: it hands the frame back to the engine instead of holding it.
These are not ranked — they are priced. Every row above is used in real shipped games. The question is never "which is correct", it is "which cost am I willing to pay for this behaviour, in this project, this week". Row (a) is the cheapest thing that works. Row (d) is the right tool the moment a single cooldown is not enough to describe the behaviour. Rows (b) and (c) sit between them.

Choosing a Timing Model

  1. Trace your own 3.2 build. If the player stood inside the radius for one second at 60 frames per second, how many projectile clones did Instantiate create — and which line of your code is responsible for that number?
  2. Why can't you call a "wait one second" function inside Update()? Describe what the player would see on screen during that wait, and explain why a game engine refuses to let you block the frame.
  3. Row (a) stores a moment; row (b) stores a duration. Which one can you print in the Console and have a player immediately understand, and which one is easier to compare against a designer's tuning value?
  4. Read the docs for InvokeRepeating. It has no idea where the player is. What has to move inside your firing method if you choose row (c), and what happens if you forget?
  5. Row (d) is described as the tool for sequences rather than single actions. What behaviour in this game is a sequence rather than a single action — and which approach do you think the boss in Unit 8 will need?
  6. Which of the four approaches lets a designer change the fire rate from the Inspector without touching code? Which of them makes that rate hard to change while the game is running?
  7. Your knob is 2 and your timestamp field was stamped at 12. What is the earliest value of Time.time at which the gate opens?
  8. Row (a) compares against Time.time; row (b) subtracts Time.deltaTime on every frame. Both measure a gap. Which of the two is tied to how often the frame runs — and which one reports the same wall-clock gap when the frame rate changes?
Build It With MeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I stop shooting too fast?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/TurretController.cs. The turret you built in 3.1 and 3.2 does not change: it still finds the target, measures the distance and spawns a projectile at the muzzle. Today adds one knob, one field and one condition. The names below are the ones this course uses — if you named yours differently in 3.1, keep your names and read the shape.

This build leaves 2 lines for you to write. Everything around them is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Add the knob and the memory to the class body

Both lines go inside the class braces and outside every method — the placement rule from 1.3, and the reason a turret can remember anything between frames at all.

    // ...the range, target and prefab fields you wrote in 3.1 and 3.2...

    [SerializeField] private float cooldown = 1.5f;

    private float lastAttackTime;
  1. 1Nothing you wrote in 3.1 or 3.2 changes today. The two lines below are the only additions to the class body.
  2. 3The knob: how many seconds must pass between shots. [SerializeField] puts it in the Inspector so a designer sets the pacing without opening your code — the same treatment you gave range and moveSpeed.It has to be a float. Shot gaps are fractions of a second, and an int would round every value you typed in the Inspector down to a whole second — so 0.5 would quietly become 0, and you would be back to a turret that fires every frame, from a type the Inspector never shows you.
  3. 5The memory. One float holding the moment, on the game clock, when this turret last fired. private, because it is the turret's own bookkeeping and no other script has any business reading it.Notice that it has no value yet — the next step gives it one. And notice where it lives. Move this line inside Update() and it would be rebuilt from nothing sixty times a second, holding the same empty value every time, and the turret could never remember a thing. That is the scope rule from 1.3: the same line in the wrong place is not a memory, it is a habit.

Step 2Seed the memory before the first frame

Start() runs once, before Update() has ever run — you already use it in 3.1 to find the target.

    void Start()
    {
        // ...the target lookup you chose in 3.1, unchanged...

        lastAttackTime = -cooldown;
    }
  1. 1The once-only setup method from 1.3. Yours already exists from 3.1, and what is inside it stays exactly as you wrote it.
  2. 3Whichever targeting approach you picked — a tag search or a serialized reference — nothing about it changes today.
  3. 5Gives the memory a first value, so the turret may fire the moment the player walks into range instead of serving a penalty for a shot it never took.Zero is a real moment on this clock. Time.time starts at 0 when the scene loads, so a field left at its default says "my last shot was at the instant the scene began" — and the gate in the next step would refuse to fire for the first cooldown seconds with the player standing right in front of it. Putting the last shot one cooldown before the game started is how you say "there has been no last shot".
  4. 6Closes Start().

Step 3Close the gate in Update()

The range check stays exactly as you wrote it in 3.1. What changes is that it is no longer the only thing deciding whether the turret fires.

    void Update()
    {
        // ...your guard and your distance measurement from 3.1...

        if (distance <= range && ______________________)
        {
            Fire();

            ________________
        }
    }
  1. 1Still the every-frame method, and still where the range check lives.
  2. 3Unchanged — the null guard, the distance, whatever you named them.
  3. Your turn5The gate. Keep the range half you already wrote, add &&, and add the second condition: the turret may fire only when enough time has passed since its last shot. Compare the game clock against that remembered moment plus your knob.The clock that only ever counts up is the Time.time row in the quick reference. The moment of the last shot is the field you declared in step 1; the gap you want is the knob. Put those three into one comparison — and ask yourself whether == could ever be true.== is the wrong operator here. Frames do not land on exact times, so the clock almost never equals your remembered moment plus the cooldown — it jumps past it. >= says at or past, which is what "enough time has passed" actually means. The && is not decoration either: drop the range half and the turret fires at nothing, on cadence, from wherever it happens to be standing.
  4. 7Your firing method from 3.2 — the one that spawns a projectile at the muzzle. Unchanged, however you named it.
  5. Your turn9The line that closes the gate again, and it runs only when a shot has actually left the barrel. Write the current moment into the field that remembers the last one.The field remembers a moment, and the gate compared it against the same clock you are standing on right now. What is the current value of that clock?This is the most common bug in the lesson. Leave it out and the gate never closes: the field keeps its old value, the condition stays true on the next frame and on every frame after it, and the turret is right back to firing at your frame rate — the bug you started today with, rebuilt inside the fix. It is also the argument for stamping the moment inside Fire() instead: any other caller of that method would skip it. Keep it here for now, where the gate and its consequence sit on the same three lines.
  6. 11Closes Update(). One more } closes the class.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • private float lastAttackTime; declared inside Update() instead of in the class body

    You will seeThe turret fires in a stream again — the 3.2 bug, unchanged — and no value you type in the Inspector makes any difference.

    Do thisDeclare it in the class body and only assign to it from inside a method. A variable declared inside a method is created fresh every time that method runs, so it cannot carry a moment from one frame to the next. Same rule as nextReportTime in 1.3.

  • the stamp line left out — nothing ever writes the new moment

    You will seeThe turret goes straight back to a stream of bullets. The condition that was meant to close the gate is still true on the next frame, and on every frame after it.

    Do thisSomething has to write the current moment at the instant the shot happens — lastAttackTime = Time.time;. It is the only line that closes the gate, and the one line in this lesson worth memorising.

  • Time.time == lastAttackTime + cooldown used instead of >=

    You will seeThe turret fires rarely, at random, or never — and turning the cooldown knob down makes it worse, which looks like the opposite of what should happen.

    Do thisUse >=. Frames do not land on exact clock values, so equality is almost never true: the clock jumps past the moment you asked for and is then unequal again.

  • the range check replaced by the cooldown check instead of combined with it

    You will seeThe turret fires on cadence at nothing, from across the map, with the player nowhere near it.

    Do thisThe two conditions combine with &&, and both have to be true. The cooldown does not replace the range test — it is attached to it.

  • a Time.time gate comparing against a field you decrement with Time.deltaTime

    You will seeThe turret fires every frame, or never, and the number in the Inspector has nothing to do with the gap you measure with a stopwatch.

    Do thisOne row, one clock. A timestamp is compared against Time.time; a countdown is the field that has Time.deltaTime subtracted from it every frame. Both are correct — in their own row. Mixing them gives you a field with two meanings and neither behaviour.

Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The two gaps are the gate condition and the stamp line, and neither is right by luck: Time.time >= lastAttackTime + cooldown because frames never land on an exact time, and lastAttackTime = Time.time; because that is the only thing that closes the gate. Your names, your range, your cooldown default and your projectile spawn from 3.2 are yours — the shape is what has to match.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/TurretController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class TurretController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float range = 6f;              // your number from 3.1
    [SerializeField] private float cooldown = 1.5f;         // the new knob
    [SerializeField] private Transform playerTransform;     // however you acquired it in 3.1
    [SerializeField] private GameObject projectilePrefab;
    [SerializeField] private Transform spawnPoint;

    private float lastAttackTime;                           // the memory: a MOMENT, not a count

    void Start()
    {
        // ...the target lookup you chose in 3.1 stays here...

        // One cooldown BEFORE the game started, so the first shot is legal
        // the moment the player walks into range.
        lastAttackTime = -cooldown;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (playerTransform == null)
        {
            return;
        }

        float distance = Vector3.Distance(transform.position, playerTransform.position);

        // Both halves must be true: in range, AND enough time since the last shot.
        if (distance <= range && Time.time >= lastAttackTime + cooldown)
        {
            Fire();

            lastAttackTime = Time.time;                     // closes the gate again
        }
    }

    private void Fire()
    {
        // ...the projectile spawn you wrote in 3.2, unchanged...
    }
}
Build Lab: Rate-Limit Your Turret ~25 min

Open Assets/Scripts/TurretController.cs — the file you built in 3.1 and 3.2. The walkthrough above built the timestamp row step by step. If that is the row you chose, you already have it working, and your remaining work is the knob's default and the proof at the bottom. If you chose the countdown, the engine schedule or the coroutine, this is where you build yours: the four decisions below are the same four for every row, and the answers look nothing alike.

Architectural specification — for whichever row you chose.

The knob (every row):

  • What serialized float lets a designer set the gap between shots from the Inspector without recompiling? What do you name it — and what does the name have to make obvious to a stranger reading your Inspector?
  • What default value will you ship, and how do you justify it against the size of the Overworld and how fast your player moves? There is no correct answer in the project — only the answer you can defend.

The memory — the decision the four rows disagree about most:

  • Row (a) keeps a moment and row (b) keeps a duration. Which does yours keep, what type is that field, and what value does it start at?
  • Row (c) keeps nothing at all. So what plays the part of the memory in your build, and who owns it — you, or the engine?
  • Row (d) keeps a handle. What is the handle for, and what can you no longer do if you lose it?
  • Whatever your row, where does that state live — inside Update() or in the class body? Say what breaks if you get it wrong, using the word "frame" in your answer.

The gate — where the rows look least alike:

  • Which two conditions must both be true before the turret may fire? Which boolean operator expresses "both"?
  • Read the docs on && and short-circuit evaluation. If the player is out of range, does Unity bother evaluating the cooldown half at all?
  • Row (c) moved the timing out of your Update() and into the engine's schedule. What has to move inside the firing method if you chose it — and where is the turret shooting while the player stands on the other side of the map if you forget?
  • Row (d) put the wait inside a coroutine. What does the loop check before each wait, and where does the range check have to live now?

The reset — the line, or its equivalent, that closes the gate:

  • In your row, what happens at the instant the turret actually fires? Which of your fields changes, and to what?
  • Predict the failure for your own row before you test it — then test it and write down whether you were right.

Proving it (every row):

  • How do you report each shot to the Console so you can count the cadence without a UI? What do you time with a stopwatch to check the number?
  • Which rows let a designer retune the rate while the game is running, and which make that hard? Test the claim you just made rather than asserting it.

Wire nothing new in the Inspector beyond your own knob. Save, press Play, and stand inside the radius. Count the Console lines for ten seconds and compare them against your knob. If you get ten lines at a two-second cooldown, the gate works.

Bug Hunt: Timer Faults

  1. Comment out the line that records the new firing time. Step into range. What does the Console look like after one second, and which earlier lesson's bug have you just rebuilt?
  2. Set your cooldown knob to 0.5 in the Inspector and test again. How many shots per second is that, and at what point does the encounter stop being hard and start being unfair?
  3. Seed your timestamp field with a large value such as 100f. How long must the player stand in range before the very first shot — and what does that tell you about what the field actually means?
  4. Set the cooldown to 0. Is a zero-second cooldown different from no cooldown at all? Which one still protects your frame budget, and which one is the bug you started with?
  5. If you chose InvokeRepeating: walk out of range mid-burst. Are projectiles still being created? Who owns the timing in that design, you or the engine?
  6. If you chose the countdown: move the decrement line inside the range check and walk out of range for ten seconds. What is the timer's value when you walk back in, and how long until the next shot?
